summary: An L-4 ground house built in 1935 and staffed until 1966, saved from demolition by the Mount Baker Club in 1982 and open to hikers today.

facts.status_note: Fell into disrepair after decommissioning; restored in 1982 by volunteers and since maintained.

access.note: Open to the public for day or overnight use, first-come first-served; no fires permitted.

visit.trail_note: Hike via Twin Lakes trailhead; steep snowfields often need an ice axe into July; road to trailhead may be impassable, adding ~2 miles; generally inaccessible early October to mid-summer due to snow.

events.note: L-4 ground house built on Winchester Mountain.

Mount Baker Club, led by Gary Haufle, obtained a special use permit and restored the lookout after it had fallen into disrepair and was slated for demolition; Forest Service provided materials, club provided labor.
Listed on the National Register of Historic Places, July 14, 1987.
Added to the National Historic Lookout Register, September 15, 1994 (date confirmed on the NHLR listing itself; Wikipedia does not state this date).

evidence.supports: Subalpine setting, views, built 1935, staffed until 1966, 1982 restoration
evidence.quote: Located in a subalpine setting within the Mt. Baker Wilderness and with views of Mt. Baker, Mt. Shuksan and the Picket Range, Winchester Mountain Lookout is a popular destination with hikers. The 14x14' L-4 ground house was built in 1935 and staffed until 1966. It fell into disrepair but in 1982 the Mt. Baker Club obtained a special use permit to restore and maintain the structure which is open to the public.

evidence.supports: Peak named by prospector Jack Post for his rifle
evidence.quote: Winchester Mountain was named in the early 1900s by prospector Jack Post for the rifle he was carrying.

evidence.supports: Built 1935, staffed until 1966, slated for demolition, 1982 Mount Baker Club deal with Gary Haufle
evidence.quote: This L-4 cab fire lookout was built in 1935 and staffed until 1966. The lookout was slated for demolition when in 1982 the Mount Baker Club, led by Gary Haufle, worked out a deal with the Forest Service to restore the lookout. The Forest Service provided the materials and the club provided all of the labor.

evidence.supports: Mount Baker Club maintains with 2 work parties a year
evidence.quote: Volunteers from the Mount Baker Club maintain the lookout with 2 work parties per year.

evidence.supports: Open to public, first-come first-served, no fires
evidence.quote: The lookout is open to the public for day or overnight use on a first-come first-served basis. Fires are not permitted at all.

evidence.supports: Two bunks, pack in pack out, no toilets, wilderness area
evidence.quote: There are 2 bunks in the lookout for overnighters. As this is a Wilderness area there are no toilet facilities at the lookout, it is strictly "Pack in, Pack out".

evidence.supports: Ice axe needed into July, road to trailhead may add 2 miles
evidence.quote: The steep snowfields usually require an ice-axe well into July. The Twin Lakes road may not be passable to the trailhead which will add 2 miles (3.2 km) to the hike.
The lookout is generally inaccessible from early October until mid summer due to snow.

notes_for_editor: Two consistent sources agree on all key dates; did not pull firelookout.com or NRHP PDF since NHLR and Wikipedia already agree closely. Access note on snow/ice-axe conditions worth flagging to editor for a seasonal access warning on the listing. Fact-check 2026-10-04: the story's September 15, 1994 NHLR date was cited only to Wikipedia, which does not state it; corrected the citation to also point to the NHLR listing itself, which does.
